text.p: British food producer Northern Foods Plc -- still smarting from losses suffered during the mad-cow crisis in 1996 -- said on Wednesday it was much more confident for the coming year and saw rapid growth in its non-milk businesses.
"We are pretty optimistic that we can stabilise the milk business and look for excellent growth on the prepared foods side," Chairman Sir Christopher Haskins told Reuters in an interview.

While its milk business profits have been nearly halved, non-milk profits have doubled in the last few years and continued to grow very rapidly, particularly in the high-quality chilled, prepared foods area, Haskins said.

The company was badly bruised last year by consumer concerns over a link between mad-cow disease (BSE) and a similar brain wasting disease in humans, as well as collapse of world prices for dairy products.

But Haskins said Northern had come to terms with its losses in beef-related products: "Its (the BSE-related loss) no worse than it was a year ago, but sales are not back to the levels of two years ago. We've come to terms with the loss of these beef products".
Northern Foods announced first-half pretax profits in November last year virtually unchanged at 57.8 million stg versus 57.2 million the previous year.
The company estimated concern over BSE had reduced operating profits by about three million sterling in the first half.
Northern Foods is due to announce full year profits for the year to March 31 in June this year, but Haskins would not comment on what was expected.

He said consumer demand for beef products was still fairly flat and estimated sales losses to Northern as a result of the BSE scare last year had been around 40 to 50 million sterling. Turnover for the six months ended September 30 was 940.8 million sterling.

The company said it expected its milk business to stabilise, having reduced the proportion of doorstep distribution to around 30 percent while supermarket distribution accounted for 45 percent, with the rest made up by smaller outlets such as grocers and restaurants.
Milk is now cheaper to buy in a British supermarket than when delivered by the old-fashioned 'milkman' to a customer's doorstep, forcing some smaller, regional dairies out of business.
Haskins said the ratio of doorstep to supermarket delivery had stabilised within Northern and was at a sustainable level and he saw considerable growth ahead in non-milk areas.
We are investing around 70 million pounds at the moment on expanding our Marks and Spencer business.
